name: Emface
lead: Emface is a facial treatment from BTL Aesthetics that delivers radiofrequency (RF) energy and high-intensity facial electrical stimulation (HIFES) through pads placed on the face. People have it done to smooth wrinkles, firm sagging skin and lift the cheeks, brows and jawline without needles, surgery or downtime.[1][2] It was launched in 2022 as the facial counterpart to BTL's Emsculpt body treatments.[2]

The RF component heats collagen and elastin fibres in the skin to prompt remodelling, while HIFES contracts facial muscles thousands of times per session to improve tone, so one treatment addresses both skin quality and the muscle layer beneath it.[1][2][3] The recommended course is four 20-minute sessions, and BTL reports best results 6 to 12 weeks after the final one.[2] A separate submental applicator targets the area under the chin.[1]

BTL reports averages of 37 percent wrinkle reduction, 30 percent more facial muscle tone and 23 percent lifting across nine studies.[2] A 2025 pre-post study in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine of 15 adults found improved forehead lift, firmness and crow's feet, with no serious adverse events, and the authors listed the small sample, lack of a control group and six-month follow-up as limitations.[3]

paras: The RF component heats the dermis to stimulate collagen remodelling, while HIFES induces contractions in facial muscles, particularly in the cheeks.[1] It is applied to the cheeks, jawline, eyebrows and forehead, and a separate submental applicator targets the area under the chin.[1] The device is described as FDA-cleared for facial wrinkles.[1]

The authors of the 2025 Siriraj Hospital study describe RF as deep tissue heating, with the dermis reaching about 40 degrees C in the first two minutes and up to 42.5 degrees C during treatment, which they say stimulates fibroblasts to form new collagen and elastin. They describe HIFES as producing supramaximal contractions of facial elevator muscles such as frontalis and zygomaticus major and minor while sparing depressors such as the masseter, and propose that strengthening these muscles lifts the forehead, brows and cheeks. They cite porcine data reporting muscle hypertrophy, with a peak facial muscle mass increase of 19.2 percent at two months, and describe the combined effect as synergistic lighting and tightening.[3]

Emface's muscle component belongs to the family of electrical muscle stimulation (EMS), in which pads near target muscles deliver impulses that mimic the action potentials normally sent by the nervous system. Wikipedia traces the first scientific evidence that electrical current can activate muscle to Luigi Galvani in 1761, and describes Soviet sport scientists using EMS in athlete training in the 1960s, with later Western results conflicting.[6] EMS is used in rehabilitation to counter muscle weakening, and Wikipedia notes FDA-mandated warnings that pacemaker wearers should not use EMS devices, and cautions around pregnancy and skin lesions.[6] That article does not address facial use.

Practical Dermatology reports the recommended protocol as four 20-minute sessions spaced 2 to 14 days apart, with no pre- or post-treatment preparation and no downtime.[2] Grokipedia gives a spacing of 5 to 10 days.[1] In the 2025 Thailand study, treatment used self-adhesive electrode pads on the forehead and both cheeks at 100 percent power, once weekly for four weeks.[3]

BTL's figures are averages of 37 percent wrinkle reduction, 30 percent facial muscle tone and 23 percent lifting, from nine clinical studies of people who completed the course.[2] For the submental applicator, Grokipedia repeats a 30.37 percent reduction in submental fat volume on MRI at three months.[1] These figures are manufacturer-linked.

The 2025 study reported no serious adverse events, and average pain scores fell from about 3.5 to about 1.6 out of 10 across sessions.[3] A broad 2025 mixed-methods analysis of non-surgical aesthetic treatments reports that complications in the category are underreported and inconsistently regulated, without being specific to Emface.[4]

A prospective, evaluator-blinded, pre-post study at Siriraj Hospital, Thailand, from September 2023 to September 2024 enrolled 15 adults (14 women, 1 man) aged 41 to 62 with mild to moderate facial and upper neck laxity, mostly Fitzpatrick skin type IV, and treated them with four weekly 20-minute sessions of synchronized RF and HIFES. Assessments were made at baseline, before the third session, and one, three and six months after the last session.[3]

Forehead lift averaged 2.14 mm at one month and 0.67 mm at six months, a statistically significant change (p = 0.0006). Cheek lift at six months, 0.58 mm, was not statistically significant (p = 0.0635). Eyebrow lift was about 1.3 mm at three and six months. Skin firmness improved by about 81 percent at six months, and crow's feet wrinkles improved by roughly 11 to 12 percent, while forehead and cheek wrinkles did not change significantly. Forehead pore volume fell by 66 percent at six months, melanin readings in some areas fell by about 3 to 3.5 percent, and volume measures were mostly unchanged. At six months, 40 percent of participants rated their improvement above 50 percent and none reported no visible improvement.[3]

The authors listed limitations: a small, mostly female sample; no control group, so placebo effects and natural aging cannot be excluded; six-month follow-up only; and no comparison with RF or HIFES alone. They suggested that peak lifting at one month may indicate that muscle tone declines over time. They also note an inconsistency between the abstract and results for cheek lift significance.[3]
A registered trial started in December 2025 combines Emface with another BTL device for temporomandibular joint pain, a medical use.[5]

card.summary: A needle-free RF plus facial-muscle-stimulation treatment whose headline numbers come from the manufacturer.

quick.overview:
Emface combines radiofrequency heating of the skin with electrical stimulation of facial muscles. It is marketed for wrinkles, muscle tone and a lifted look.

The quoted results come from manufacturer-linked data; no independent trials were found.
quick.mechanism: RF energy heats the dermis to stimulate collagen remodeling, while stimulation induces facial muscle contractions.
quick.risks: No Emface-specific safety data were found. A 2025 study of non-surgical aesthetic treatments generally reports that complications are underreported.

chain: Pads deliver RF heat to the dermis and electrical pulses to facial muscles
Collagen remodelling is prompted and muscles contract repeatedly
Skin looks firmer and cheeks, brows and forehead sit higher
angle.text: Emface is used as a non-surgical lift. Clients book a short course of 20-minute sessions hoping for tighter-looking skin and a subtle raising of the brows and cheeks, with no recovery period.
